## 1. Identification Strategy  
Difference-in-Differences (DID).  
• Two cross-sections of the same restaurants (before vs. after).  
• Clear policy shock that applies to one state only.  
• Parallel-trends assumption is testable (to some extent) with pre-period data from PA vs. NJ and with observable covariates.  
Given the small number of time periods, DID is more transparent than an event study and does not require an instrument or a forcing variable.

---

## 2. Treatment and Control  
Treatment variable  
  Treated = 1 if restaurant is located in New Jersey AND observation date ≥ 1 Apr 1992; 0 otherwise.  
Control group  
  Restaurants in eastern Pennsylvania during the same calendar months.  
Timing  
  Treatment starts 1 Apr 1992. Pre-period: survey wave 1 (Feb–Mar 1992). Post-period: survey wave 2 (Nov–Dec 1992).  
RDD elements?  
  None—no running variable.

---

## 3. Key Identifying Assumptions  

1. Parallel trends: In the absence of the NJ increase, employment in NJ and PA fast-food outlets would have evolved similarly between Feb–Mar and Nov–Dec 1992.  
   • Plausible because the stores are geographically contiguous, sell standardized products, and face similar macro conditions.  
   • Can be probed using chain-level controls and by comparing pre-1992 trends from administrative data (if obtainable).  

2. No spillovers/contamination: PA stores were not indirectly affected (e.g., via labor mobility or changes in demand).  
   • Reasonably plausible: commuting across the Delaware River exists but is modest for low-wage teenagers.  
   • Will test robustness by dropping PA counties immediately adjacent to NJ.  

3. Stable composition (SUTVA): The set of jobs measured and reporting quality are unchanged; attrition is not systematically related to treatment.  
   • 15 % attrition is modest but will be addressed via balanced-panel analysis and IPW weights.  

4. No anticipation: Stores did not adjust employment between Feb and Mar in expectation of the April 1 change.  
   • The 4–6-week interval between announcement and implementation was short; still, we will test for anticipatory cuts in February data using daily hours (if available).

---

## 4. Main Threats and Mitigation  

Threat 1: Differential demand shocks (e.g., a local recession in PA).  
  Action:  
  • Include county-by-time unemployment controls.  
  • Chain fixed effects and county fixed effects where sample size allows.  

Threat 2: Attrition bias.  
  Action:  
  • Re-estimate on balanced panel (restaurants observed in both waves).  
  • Inverse-probability weighting based on observables that predict survey response.  

Threat 3: Spillovers or labor-supply substitution.  
  Action:  
  • Drop PA outlets within 15 miles of the NJ border (leave-one-out test).  
  • Report DID estimates with vs. without border counties.

---

## 5. R Code Outline (executable)

```r
# Load libraries
library(data.table)   # fast data manipulation
library(fixest)       # regression with multi-way clustering
library(ggplot2)

# 1. Load data
dt <- fread("fastfood_nj_pa.csv")  # file with both waves appended row-wise

# 2. Variable construction
dt[, post := as.integer(date >= as.Date("1992-04-01"))]   # treatment timing
dt[, nj   := as.integer(state == "NJ")]                   # treatment group
dt[, treat_post := post * nj]                             # DID term

# Construct FTE employment:
# Suppose we have variables: FT_workers, PT_workers, Hours_PT
dt[, fte := FT_workers + (Hours_PT / 40)]                 # PT hours / 40

# Balanced panel indicator
dt[, obs_count := .N, by = id]               # id is restaurant id
dt[, balanced  := as.integer(obs_count == 2)]

# 3. Main DID specification
did_main <- feols(fte ~ treat_post | id + post + chain,     # two-way FE
                  data = dt,
                  cluster = "id")      # cluster at restaurant level
summary(did_main)

# 4. Robustness: balanced panel only
did_bal <- feols(fte ~ treat_post | id + post + chain,
                 data = dt[balanced == 1],
                 cluster = "id")
summary(did_bal)

# 5. Robustness: remove PA border counties
border_pa <- c("Bucks","Northampton","Delaware")  # example list
did_noborder <- feols(fte ~ treat_post | id + post + chain,
                      data = dt[!(state=="PA" & county %in% border_pa)],
                      cluster = "id")
summary(did_noborder)

# 6. Simple visualization
ggplot(dt[, .(fte = mean(fte)), by = .(post, state)]) +
  geom_line(aes(x = factor(post), y = fte, color = state, group = state)) +
  labs(x = "Post-period (=1)", y = "Mean FTE Employment")
```

---

## 6. Expected Results  
Standard competitive-model prior: a binding 19 % wage hike should reduce low-skill employment. With a typical teen labor demand elasticity of −0.1 to −0.3, a 19 % price increase implies roughly −2 % to −6 % employment. I therefore expect the DID coefficient on `treat_post` to be negative, around −0.3 to −1.5 FTE per store (≈ −5 % to −10 %).

---

## 7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)  
(1 = clearly satisfied, 0 = questionable)  

C1: Parallel pre-trends supported by data …………………… 0.5  
C2: No differential shocks affecting only treatment ………… 0.5  
C3: No spillovers or interference …………………………………… 0.5  
C4: Stable composition / no attrition bias ………………… 0.5  
C5: Treatment correctly assigned, no contamination ……… 1.0  

Total ≈ 3.0 / 5 — reasonable but not iron-clad.
